title: Ovadia Yosef: Restore the Crown
hook: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef set out to restore Sephardi law and custom to its full dignity
carry: restore the crown: your own sages, with honor
tomorrow: a Moroccan sage people lined up to see. what did they ask him for?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabazi's songs held joy and longing in one tune. Poetry of Yemen. Today, a rabbi who wanted a whole community's old ways to stand up straight again.

A family recipe gets "updated" by a cousin who thinks the original was old-fashioned. A grandmother's accent gets corrected at school. Small things, until one day the old way is gone and nobody quite decided to lose it. One question for today: what do you owe the ways of the people who raised you? Rabbi Ovadia Yosef had an answer, and he borrowed a phrase from the Talmud to say it: restore the crown to its former glory. Why a crown?

segments.voice: Here's the fact to tell a friend: the phrase began as praise for God. In the Talmud, tractate Yoma, the sages explain that the Men of the Great Assembly earned their name because they restored God's full praise, great, mighty and awesome, after earlier prophets had left words out. They restored the crown to its former glory. Rabbi Ovadia Yosef took that phrase for his life's work. He wanted Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, whose families came from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, to keep the rulings and customs of their own sages with full confidence, not as a lesser version of someone else's. A crown isn't new. It's something you already own, put back where it belongs. Underneath is the Torah's own answer to today's question: "Honour thy father and thy mother." Honor reaches past two people to the ways they handed you. Now a neighbor who says this too. Christians read the same commandment, and Paul's letter to the Ephesians repeats it: "Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise." Shared ground, word for word. And an honest difference. Ephesians places it in a letter to Christian households, telling children to obey their parents "in the Lord," read in the light of Christ. In Jewish tradition it stands as one of the Torah's commandments, and the rabbis spell out its details, from serving a parent food to not sitting in their seat. Rabbi Ovadia stretched that honor to a whole community's inheritance. Restore the crown.

segments.voice: Find one object that came to you from someone older: a candlestick, a recipe card, a photo, a ring, even a phrase they always said. Hold it or look at it for the whole sit, as if setting it back in its place. Name to yourself one way of theirs you want to keep.

segments.voice: Restore the crown: Rabbi Ovadia Yosef's phrase, from the Talmud's praise of God. Put back what you already own, with honor.
Your line: restore the crown, your own sages, with honor. What you put back was yours all along. See you tomorrow.
